title: FRCS Ophthalmology Viva & Clinical Exams: Candidate Experiences & Key Learnings (2024-2025)
summary: This comprehensive poster distills the FRCS Ophthalmology exam experiences of multiple candidates from 2024-2025, offering invaluable insights into the viva and clinical stations. Covering a wide array of ophthalmic topics and general medical emergencies, it highlights common questions, expected answers, crucial examination techniques, and strategic preparation advice for aspiring fellows.

sections.title: Exam Logistics & Preparation Pearls
content: FRCS in second attempt (Bangalore slot, Feb 2025) after first time at Mumbai (Nov 2024).
Goal: Not to make those mistakes from the first exam.
Acknowledgement: Blessings of Lord Sri Ram, family support (especially wife Dr. Chinmayee, Glaucoma consultant), Prof. Dr. Muthusamy sir for moral support.
Candidate re-started preparing and joined MVUPGO 10 days before the exam.
Day-1 Orals/OSCE @ Sheraton Grand Hotel, Bangalore, Feb 4th, 2025.
Only two candidates attended in the afternoon post-lunch session that day – very rare.
Each station features case scenario text / color clinical photographs printed on a page.
Big hall with three tables for each station, two examiners sitting together, with sets of scenarios.
Three candidates can take the exam at a time, one at each station.
Be prepared for voice/noise from adjacent tables, must ignore them.
Dress code: Formal dress only (suit & tie/full sleeve/short sleeve shirts, avoid jeans). Analog watches allowed.

Each station: Set of questions (up to 6) related to a particular scenario. Each examiner gives 2-3 scenarios in 10 minutes (half of the time in that station). After 10 minutes, the second examiner takes over.
P.S. Don’t feel that you have already answered enough questions and don’t take it lightly for the rest of the questions. Examiner marking details are at the end of the experience.
Questions relate to common scenarios seen routinely, don’t expect tricky or rare answers.
**VIVA Answering Tips:**
i) Take a few seconds when given a scenario, answer to the point.
ii) Answer in a framed manner.
iii) Don’t be in a hurry to answer/blabber with the time factor in mind.
iv) Maintain eye contact, be polite, never argue.

v) Don’t be preoccupied with one answer for a scenario (e.g., shallow AC with high IOP – don’t only think of Malignant Glaucoma; consider other clues like 'middle-aged hyperope' for closed-angle glaucoma discussion).
vi) Don’t get overjoyed or depressed with performance at each station. Passing in all stations is important.

sections.title: Dr. Vishnu Teja Gonugunta's FRCS Experience (Feb 2025)
sections.content: This section details the FRCS (Glasgow) experience of Dr. Vishnu Teja Gonugunta, MS, FAEH, FCMS, FAICO (Cornea), Consultant at Modern Eye Hospital & Research Centre, Nellore, India, who cleared the exam in his second attempt in February 2025.

sections.title: Station-3 (General Medicine, Emergency, Neuro-ophthalmology, Motility) - Day 1 Orals
sections.content: Examiner was a male, possibly Japanese, very serious looking. This station was not so great as I was not sure whether I answered what he was expecting and didn’t get some of the questions asked.

sections.title: General Medicine and Medical Emergencies
content: **1. Hypoglycaemia Treatment:**
Me: Followed Oxford Handbook of Medicine: orange juice to dextrose solution 10% in semiconscious or unconscious, including the drip rate.
Examiner 1: What if no IV access or fluids not available?
Me: IM glucagon.
**2. Seizures Treatment:**
Me: Check for A, B, C; rule out hypoglycaemia, alcoholism. Lorazepam - dose mentioned.
**3. Diabetes Mellitus Macroangiopathy Manifestations:**
Me: DVT/foot gangrene; cardiac.
**4. How DM Can Affect the Eye:**
Me: Dry eye to PDR, vitreous hemorrhage and neovascular glaucoma, vascular occlusions.
**5. Side Effects of OHA (Oral Hypoglycemic Agents):**
Examiner 1: Lactic acidosis and hypoglycaemia common with which drugs?
Me: Metformin causes lactic acidosis and sulfonylureas causes hypoglycaemia.

sections.title: Neuro-ophthalmology, Strabismus, and Ocular Motility
content: **1. Duane's Retraction Syndrome:**
Photograph given. Asked the types of DRS.
What type of surgery? Me: Recession may be done and resections to be avoided.
**2. Amblyopia Management:**
Studies related to amblyopia. Patching vs atropine which is better etc were asked.
**3. Esotropia in a Child:**
Photograph shown. Esotropia classification.

sections.title: Station 1 (Anterior Segment, Orbit, Oculoplasty, Tumors) - Day 1 Orals
sections.content: Both the examiners were Indian. Very pleased with their attitude and behaviour. Very welcoming doctors.

sections.title: Corneal Edema with Thinning (Acute Hydrops)
content: **1. Diagnosis:**
Examiner 1: Clinical photograph of corneal edema with thinning shown - what could be the diagnosis?
Me: Acute hydrops.
**Probable Causes, Treatment, Possible Age:**
Me: Keratoconus, pellucid.
Conservative management with topical steroids, cycloplegics, hyperosmotics, IOP lowering mentioned.
Penetrating keratoplasty also mentioned.

sections.title: Refractive Surprise Post-Surgery (-3.5 DS)
content: **2. Cause? What next?**
Me: (Capsular distension syndrome in mind) but wrongly mentioned it as capsular block syndrome (which happens intraoperatively).
Examiner 1: (Stares.... looked like expecting for a better answer).
Me: Possible error in IOL calculation; to check A-scan calibration; check whether all patients are having similar surprise.

sections.title: Black Elevated Iris Mass (Iris Melanoma)
content: **3. Clinical photograph of black elevated iris mass 4x4 mm at pupillary margin. Causes. What will you do?**
Me: Looks like an Iris melanoma, would like to do dilated examination to look for posterior uvea involvement. Sectoral iridectomy could suffice as angle is not involved. (Examiner looked satisfied).

sections.title: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus
content: **4. Clinical photograph of Herpes zoster. Discussion went about what do you want to examine, causes and treatment:**

Me: (With gross examination without slit lamp) - want to look for bells phenomenon, lesions over the mastoid area) to look for Ramsay-Hunt syndrome, cranial nerve palsies and then cornea examination etc.

sections.title: Lagophthalmos & Facial Nerve Palsy
content: **5. Clinical picture of lagophthalmos was shown. Causes and treatment?**
Me: Facial nerve palsy. I was telling about the various causes from the table in AAO BCSC (neuro-opthal volume facial nerve palsy table).
Examiner 2: Most common cause would be?
Me: Cerebellopontine angle tumor. (Examiner was waiting for this).
Examiner 2: What’s the name of the tumor?
Me: Then I said schwannoma/Acoustic Neuroma. Examiner smiled and looked very happy to hear that.
Treatment with lubricants and lid taping and gold implants were also part of the discussion.

sections.title: Station 2 (Posterior Segment) - Day 1 Orals
sections.content: This station focused on fundus evaluations, macular degeneration, and glaucoma-related diagnostics.

sections.title: Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD) Scenario
content: **1. Fundus picture shown (Right Eye):**
Me: Clinical fundus photograph of the right eye with good media clarity, normal disc and vessels with yellowish white lesions in the macula possibly Age related macular degeneration.
**What next?**
Me: Vision, BCVA, Amsler grid testing to look for metamorphopsia, fundus photograph and OCT to look for changes and followup.
**What to tell the patient?**
Me: Conservatively avoiding UV light, so to use UV filter glasses, Stop smoking, use antioxidants as per AREDS 2.
**What's AREDS 2?**
Me: Told every details about Composition and dose in detail. (Examiner wanted the composition in detail).
**AREDS 2 Composition:** Vitamin C 500 mg, Vitamin E 400 IU, Copper 2 mg, Zinc 80 mg, Lutein 10 mg and Zeaxanthin 2 mg.
**Diet Recommendation?**
Me: I was not very sure of this answer (though fruits and green leafy vegetables were running in my mind) I stayed calm. He passed to next question.

sections.title: Applanation Tonometry Errors
content: **2. What are the possible errors in Applanation tonometry?**
Me: Told everything I knew of.
i. Calibration of the applanation tonometer.
ii. Overstaining will cause thick fluorescein mire – over estimation of IOP.
iii. Understaining will cause thin mires and under estimation of IOP.
iv. Scarred corneas will give erroneous results.
v. Dry eye.

vi. In case of astigmatism – we have to take average of the readings of applanation prism placed vertically and horizontally or alternatively keeping the red line in the prism in line with the flat corneal meridian (examiner looked fine).

sections.title: Retinal Detachment (RD) & Management
content: **3. Tell about this (Wide angle color fundus picture):**
Me: It’s a wide angle color fundus picture showing large superior retinal detachment involving the macula. Identified the horseshoe tear.
**What do you want to do?**
Me: Need to take him for vitreo retinal surgery – pars plana vitrectomy with subretinal fluid drainage, with endolaser with fluid air exchange and silicone oil or gas tamponade.
**Advantages of gas and silicone oil:**
Me: In multiple breaks and PVR silicone oil is better. Gas is better for superior RD. To be avoided when patient wants to travel by air.

sections.title: Postop Trabeculectomy Complication: Shallow AC & Low IOP
content: **4. Scenario of immediate postop trabeculectomy – shallow AC and low IOP of 4 mm of Hg. Causes and what to do?**
Me: Bleb leak or over filtration. To look for seidel test.
Examiner 2: In which case Seidel will be positive?
Me: Bleb leak.

sections.title: Glaucomatous Disc Assessment & Management
content: **5. Picture of a glaucomatous disc:**
Me: Told the findings. Cup disc ratio of 0.7 with bayoneting sign.
**How do you proceed?**
Me: IOP check, pachymetry, visual field assessment by HFA and AGM therapy.
**Preferred AGM and why?**
Me: Prostaglandin analogues – for better compliance with one time dosage and no systemic side effects.

I was not asked many questions here. This was my last station. I don’t want to give up at any moment. So was waiting for more. Examiner smiled and stayed calm. There was still time to finish, so was just sitting quiet, when the first examiner offered me to have a candy from a cup placed on the table, till the time finishes. So nice of him . It made me feel even more comfortable!

sections.title: Day-2 Clinicals (Narayana Nethralaya, Bengaluru, Feb 6th, 2025)
sections.content: This section covers the clinical examination stations on the second day of the FRCS exam.

sections.title: Station 3 (Neuro-ophthalmology and Motility) - Clinicals
sections.content: There were two Indian examiners. One was there in orals for Anterior segment, who was encouraging in viva, but very neutral here. The other new Indian examiner looked very serious and strict.

sections.title: Visual Fields and Pupillary Examination
content: **1. Check visual fields for this patient and do examine her pupils (Elderly female 50-60 years):**
I have carried my examination things which included a red pin for neuro station. Used the white pin from the hospital for peripheral field.
Always use a bright light with room lights dimmed for pupillary examination - did the same.
i. Greeted the patient (“Hello madam!”) and gave a smile to her to comfort her.
ii. After the patient was seated in the chair unit, I sat in a revolving stool opposite to her, adjusted my height to have same eye levels.
iii. Did confrontation fields first with both eyes and then with each eye:
a. “To fix at my nose”.
b. Any part of my face appears missing or blurred.
c. Check if the patient can see fingers presented in front her eye.
d. Then fingers presented in four quadrants, keeping other eye closed.
e. Repeat with other eye.
f. Noted the defect in right eye inferonasal quadrant, rest all normal in both eyes.
g. Did peripheral field examination first with my red pin.
h. Did central field examination with a white pin available there.
iv. Pupillary examination:
a. Dimmed the room lights – asked a helper there.
b. Used a bright torch light to check direct and consensual light reflex in both eyes separately.
c. RAPD was noted in the right eye where field defect was noted.
d. Didn’t check pupillary examination on convergence.
**Examiner-1: What is your inference?**

Me: There is inferonasal visual field defect with RAPD in her right eye. I would like to check her vision, BCVA, slitlamp examination especially for fundus and Humphrey visual fields (unilateral optic nerve lesions was my suspicion, may be optic neuritis) and if required neuroimaging.

(Later I got to know from other candidate that the patient had a Hemi-retinal vein occlusion with unilateral nasal field defect superior and inferior, luckily during my examination the patient said only one quadrant - which obviously the examiner had considered).

P.S. I took lot of time for this case, but I took my time to follow the correct technique even after crossing half the time ~10 minutes, examiner was also not in hurry for other examiner to take over.

sections.title: Ocular Motility & Third Nerve Palsy
content: **2. Examiner-2: Check ocular motility for this patient (young lady 20-25 years with left eye complete ptosis):**
Me: Can I start with Hirschberg test.
Examiner-2: Ok.
Me:
 Retracted her left ptotic lid,
 Checked corneal reflex test with a torch- there was gross exotropia.
 For motility check:
a. (I carried my fixation target) asked her whether she can see the target first, I was still retracting her completely ptotic lid.
b. Checked motility in the standard pattern after coming to center.
c. Complete third nerve palsy involving pupil. There was limitation of adduction, elevation and depression (all -4).
**What are the possible causes?**
Me: Trauma.
Examiner-2: No history of trauma. What else?
Me: Trying to recall the Kanski pages of third nerve palsy, nuclear lesions and syndromes – but they don’t fit here (I was running out of time).
Examiner-2: Probable cause which is life threatening.
Me: Carotid cavernous fistula.
Examiner-2: (Startled).
Me: But there will be other cranial nerves involvement too.
Examiner-2: Check fourth cranial nerve for her.

Me: (I retracted her left ptotic lid, asked her to look towards her nose from distance fixation to elicit the intorsion) “It’s there. So, it’s not CCF” I said. Suddenly I remembered aneurysm. So I said out “Aneurysm of the third cranial nerve”.
Examiner stood calm. Times up. The other examiner gave a small smile, assuring me!
Could examine only 2 cases, but no regrets. I wanted to perform well and I was satisfied in this station. I wanted to concentrate fresh for the next station and do well.

sections.title: Station 4 (Orbit, Lids and Oculoplasty) - Clinicals
sections.content: One of the examiner was the ?Japanese one who was there for my neuro viva. I was a bit depressed to see him, but tried to be afresh. The other examiner was an Indian.

sections.title: Examine Proptosis (Thyroid Eye Disease)
content: **1. Examiner 1: Examine this patient (middle-aged male 50 years with right eye proptosed eye with congestion):**
Me: There is proptosis of right eye with diffuse congestion.
**Measure proptosis. (Given Hertel exophthalmometer):**
Me: 23 mm in right eye, 16 mm in left eye.
**What do you want to do?**
Me: This could be thyroid eye disease. I want to take history.
**What history?**
Me: Wanted to express my knowledge – so trying to tell about systemic findings – like pretibial myxedema, nails.
Examiner 1: (Examiner was reluctant as soon as he heard ‘systemic’, he wanted something else) WHAT ELSE?
Me: I wanted to do orbit examination!
Examiner 1: Do it!
Me: (I was very happy to hear this. I wanted to demonstrate that as I read it well and practised many times) checking the orbital margins, checking pulsation/thrill/retropulsion/lymph nodes/thyroid.
**WHAT ELSE?**
Me: I want to look for corneal sensations/lagophthalmos/Bells, slitlamp examination especially fundus, IOP.
**WHAT ELSE?**
Me: Cranial nerve examination especially second and third cranial nerve like vision, color vision pupil examination, extraocular motility and field testing.
Examiner 1: (He wanted this) Do it.
Me: Pupil has RAPD in right eye, mild movement restriction.
**Plan?**
Me: Thyroid function tests, orbit imaging and plan for orbit decompression (starting lateral or medial wall) apart from conservative management.
Time was already past half the time. He still wanted to continue. Then gave up. Other examiner took over.

sections.title: Ptosis: Aponeurotic vs. Congenital
content: **2. Examiner 2: See this case:**
Me: I had a predetermined mind to see the patient from the distance to notice old lady with left eye ptosis. I said aloud “left aponeurotic ptosis”.
Examiner 2: See the other eye.
Me: There was dilated pupil. Movements restricted. (Actual problem was in right eye).
**Why aponeurotic?**
Me: Crease was high and due to age.
**Measure it:**
Me: (Started with corneal reflex, MRD 1 and MRD 2 and levator function, when I realised there is no lid crease) no lid crease possibly congenital as well (examiner smiled).
There was not much discussion. Time is already up. I was feeling like ok station.

sections.title: Station 1 (Anterior Segment including Glaucoma) - Clinicals
sections.content: A different slit lamp, took time to understand and use. Someone guided me how to use the slit lamp too.

sections.title: Anterior Segment Cases
content: **1. Examiner 1: See this case:**
Me: Pseudoexfoliation on lens capsule (no further viva).
**2. Examiner 1: See this case:**
Me: Pseudophakia. I couldn’t make out anything else. After searching found a Surgical PI, retracted lid to find a bleb. I said “Post trabeculectomy looks failed”.
**Why failed bleb?**
Me: Vascular and no elevation of the bleb.
**3. Examiner 2: See this case:**

Me: Left eye was completely normal. In right eye there was peripheral anterior synechiae temporally 2-3 clock hours with mild overlying stromal edema; rest of the cornea clear; what could be it due to?
Me: Trauma, chronic uveitis, history of any surgery done or LASER PI.
Examiner 2: No h.o trauma; what else?
Me: (After thinking for a while) Finally said it could be ‘Axenfeld-Reiger syndrome’, would like to look for dental anomalies! Examiner looked satisfied. DD should be ICE syndrome as well.

sections.title: Ophthalmo DDx: Peripheral Anterior Synechiae with Stromal Edema

rows: Corectopia, iris stromal hypoplasia, dental anomalies (microdontia, anodontia), glaucoma
Corneal endothelial abnormalities (hammered silver appearance), iris atrophy, glaucoma, corectopia, ectropion uveae
History of injury, signs of previous trauma (e.g., iridodialysis, angle recession)
Recurrent inflammation, KPs, posterior synechiae (may progress to PAS), band keratopathy
History of intraocular surgery (e.g., PI with excessive peripheral placement), inflammation related to surgery

sections.title: Station 2 (Posterior Segment) - Clinicals
sections.content: The two Indian examiners were there for posterior segment and anterior segment. Elderly lady examiner (Dr. Paul) very good and Male Dr. Datta I think both were very good, supportive. He assisted me in taking the instruments, switching lights. Very cool examiners.

sections.title: Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) & Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP)
content: **1. Examiner-1: Do slit lamp biomicroscopy for fundus for this patient right eye:**

Me: Commented on media, disc, vessels, background – Hemorrhages, IRMA at one quadrants, and NVE at one area – I said it is looking like – Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy – Would like to examine other eye, vision testing, glucose levels check and FFA/OCT and then plan for need for PRP (not much discussion).
**2. Examiner-2: Do indirect ophthalmoscopy for this patient (60-year-old lady):**

Me: (This is probably the last case of my exam. I was excited at the same time worried. Patient was a 60 year old lady) Posterior pole looked fairly normal with mild disc pallor and arteriolar narrowing and perivenous pigmentation were there scattered. First I said it looked like PRP laser marks and then on other eye examination I said it is bony spicules probably Retinitis Pigmentosa.
**What next?** (Examiner looked satisfied with the RP answer though)
Me: Vision check, guarded prognosis if she undergoes cataract surgery. Low vision aids if nothing helps.

sections.title: Dr. Muhammad Ahsen's FRCS Experience (April 2024)
sections.content: Dr. Muhammad Ahsen from Pakistan, MBBS, FCPS (ophth), FRCS (Glasgow) (ophth), currently working in MOH-Kuwait, cleared FRCS Glasgow in his first attempt at Amman (Jordan) on April 24. All praise to Allah Almighty. Did FCPS training at Allied Hospital Faisalabad.

sections.title: Study Sources - Dr. Ahsen
content: 1. Kanski
2. Oxford Ophthalmology Handbook
3. Emergency Medicine Oxford Handbook
4. Past experiences at Amman Center.
5. Eye wiki on google :)

sections.title: OSCE (23-4-24) - Dr. Ahsen
sections.content: This section covers the OSCE (Objective Structured Clinical Examination) portion of Dr. Ahsen's exam.

sections.title: Anterior Segment/Lids Adnexa/Oculoplastic - OSCE
content: **1. Papilloma photo at lower lid:**
The First Examiner asked to describe findings and give differentials then possible diagnoses, causes, and treatment options.
**2. After uneventful phaco surgery the patient has -2.00D refractive error:**
Causes, management options. Told all in detail for early and late management.
**3. Scenario of a child with congenital ptosis + Marcus Gunn Jaw winking phenomenon:**
Asked for management options.
**Second examiner:**
**1. Signs of PCR while phaco emulsification and management in each step detailed discussion.**
**2. Lattice dystrophy photo:**
Description & give differentials, usual symptoms of patients having lattice-like RCE management, and finally keratoplasty options.
**3. Scenario of the patient having one-day old eye injury with broken glass:**

A detailed discussion of ruptured globe/IOFB management, investigations especially how to repair Corneo-Scleral tear. Where to apply first suture, which suture and exploration to look for the posterior extent of tear.

sections.title: Posterior Segment - OSCE
content: **First examiner:**
**1. A photo of a thin avascular bleb overhanging limbus without PI in the photo may be the bleb was obscuring P.I.:**

Particularly asked why the bleb is thin/avascular. I told could be due to the MMC application. Description of bleb, functional/non-functional bleb. Detailed discussion of post-trabeculectomy complications.
**2. Photo of NVG with extensive rubeosis iridis:**
Causes & management options. I stated that management depends on visual potential then discussed every possible scenario accordingly.
**3. Humphery Visual field 24-2 photo with paracentral scotomas:**
Started describing reliability indices and the testing algorithms then he asked what is SITA FAST? why? Told the answer quicker/reliable and the bell rang.
**Second examiner:**
**1. Simply asked in BRVO what are your concerns in such patients?**
Told in detail about the causes and management of CME and systemic risk factors management to prevent ischemia and NVG in eye as well as cardiovascular complications.
**2. Scenario of metamorphopsia and blurred vision in 80years old lady:**
Differentials and then discussion of macular hole management at all stages.
**3. Retinitis pigmentosa fundus photo:**
Description and causes of poor vision in RP patients, told all causes from anterior segment to posterior segment.

sections.title: Neuro Motility and General Medicine - OSCE
content: **Medicine examiner:**
**1. Graves ophthalmopathy:**
Causes especially Pathophysiology and systemic signs other than ocular features. Treatment options.
**2. Typical scenario of IIH with fundus photo of papilledema:**
Investigations and management options. Don't forget to refer to neurology and neuropathologist for ON fenestration or VP shunting by a neurosurgeon for persistent symptoms.
**3. Scenario of patient having Grand mal seizures:**
Causes and management.
**Second examiner (expressionless guy):**
**1. Fundus photo of swollen optic disc with female having blurred vision and pain on eye movements:**
Optic neuritis, causes other than demyelinating.
**2. 40 year old male with sudden headache and unilateral ptosis but when he lifts his eyelid he complains of double vision:**

DDs: 3rd nerve palsy vs horner syndrome. Definite dx: 3rd nerve but examiner on my station was insisting for horner syndrome not in mood of discussing why its not horner. But i agreed at the end ok if you say its horner ok then let it be. But my top differential was 3rd nerve palsy. Then he asked the surgical and medical causes of 3rd nerve palsy and investigations.
**3. Photo of intermittent exotropia with time to time outward deviation of eyes of 8 years old boy noted by the parents recently:**
Management options in detail.
Alhamdulillah done with OSCE. Overall i was happy that i would inshallah get through.

sections.title: Clinical Examination (25-4-24) - Dr. Ahsen
sections.content: Here comes the big day where you actually realise that time flies really quickly 😂 😂

sections.title: Posterior Segment - Clinical Examination
content: **Case-1. Examine the posterior segment of left eye patient sitting on slit lamp:**

I started examining from anterior to posterior as the patient had corneal graft, aphakic and siliconized eye with flat retina and pale optic disc and peripheral laser marks. It was a case of post-op gunshot injury (ruptured globe + IOFB/RRD). Asked about the findings and status of retina attached or detached. Complications of silicon oil.
**Case-2) Command of posterior segment examination of left eye of old age male patient with indirect ophthalmoscope..:**

Pupil was mid dilated and patient was pseudophakic but with good view. It was post op PPV TRD/VH with endolaser marks at peripheral retina and dull foveal reflex, pale optic disc + fibrous bands around disc. Usual questions of ppv indications and complications.
**Case-3) A young boy sitting on a slit lamp with Stargardt’s disease with exotropia in right eye:**
I just described optic disc (slight pallor) findings and a dull reflex of macula & the bell rang. Couldn’t complete the case and the examiner seemed satisfied already.

sections.title: Neuro-Ophthalmic & Motility Disorders - Clinical Examination
content: **Case-1: Young girl with glasses having Good alternating Esotropia:**

Command was to do the motility examination. I started with VA-Hirschberg-cover/uncover @ distance and near with and without glasses. And finally, EOM with saccades and convergence. 6 minutes passed so quickly that just 1 question was asked: what's the diagnosis? I said alternating esotropia but i need to take history he said its since birth then I told ok its infantile esotropia. He asked what about the glasses, i said there could be refractive error. He nodded & examiner seemed satisfied.
**Case-2: The worst case as i still couldn’t understand what was the actual problem with that lady. 😛 a hard nut to crack! Middle aged lady sitting on slit lamp:**

Command: Examine the pupils, anterior segment of both eyes and fundus exam in undilated Pupils. I Started off with dim light pupil examination and found bilateral brisk response pupils no RAPD, Just anisocoria in dark. right pupil was a bit larger in size I thought it could be Adie’s pupil that's why he is asking for slit lamp examination to look for vermiform movements But honestly there was no such thing... ant segment was perfectly fine, examiner asked to quickly see the fundus: Bilateral large discs with healthy NRR, CDR almost 0.8 Ou. Described the disc findings and the bell rang. While leaving the room he showed me the OCT ONH and asked does this patient have glaucoma? I quickly had a look at OCT printout and made sure that the cup was symmetrical in size and there was no RNFL loss and quickly responded as per clinical exam findings and OCT printout that there was no sign of glaucoma. No comments from the examiner as he was expressionless again but i had seen him marking tick on the fail side column 😜 This case gave me nightmares till the result date. Honestly i might have missed some findings..

sections.title: Oculoplasty - Clinical Examination
content: **Case-1. Young girl sitting on chair with right eye mild ptosis and 15 degree exotropia and bilateral congested looking eyes:**

Command was to inspect and tell findings, Then do the right eye ptosis measurements, did all parameters like VA(NPL in right eye) pupil examination (eccentric pupil) pseudophakic right eye, MRD1, PFH, LF,-and at the end checked the bell’s phenomenon which was really poor in both eyes. I wanted to check EOM but examiner refused & said no need. Question was what would you do for this patient? I replied i would like to take history and examine the patient on slit lamp and counsel the patient and would observe and consider conservative treatment options as the patient had poor bell’s phenomenon. Would you do surgery? I said NO.
**Case-2: Old lady with left eye cicatricial ectropion with chemical injury on left side of the face:**

Described the findings while examining the patient, palpated the scar and lid laxity tests as there was also horizontal lid laxity present then I asked to see the patient on a slit lamp as well. Told the Management options as usual written in the books. Ok now examine the other eye of the same lady, there was right eye sebaceous cyst below the superotemporal orbital margin, did all methods of cyst examination. What are your differentials and management? Told excision biopsy and histopathological examination afterwards.
**Case-3) Slit lamp examination of left eye of young male:**

I could only describe the findings in the given time which were; Lower lid trichiasis touching the globe with symblepharon obscuring the lower punctum +Bulbar congestion and corneal scarring, Lid margin was normal no entropion noted. & The bell rang.
Alhamdulillah Oculoplasty station was satisfactory as I managed to see one extra case.

sections.title: Anterior Segment - Clinical Examination
content: **Case-1: Young girl around 15 years old sitting on slit lamp:**

Command was to examine the anterior segment of left eye: It was a case of CAU with band keratopathy, could be JRA. Findings were: Pseudophakic, seclusio pupilae, iris bombe, KPs, AC cells +1, peripheral iridocorneal touch 360 degree. Questions were Differentials, Causes of band keratopathy in non inflammatory conditions other than ocular causes.
**Case-2. Young male on slit lamp:**

Command was to examine the anterior segment of left eye then right eye. Left eye: failed keratoplasty graft every hazy view of the AC with superficial and deep vascularization and anterior staphyloma at 6 O’clock away from graft host junction. Some sutures were also removed. I was asked is the patient phakic or aphakic? I replied i cant comment because there is no view-he smiled and said fair enough. OK examine the right eye: It was perfectly fine normal Clear cornea: quiet ac No sign of keratoconus. He asked is there any sign of keratoconus i said as per my examination of anterior segment there is no sign of keratoconus. He agreed. Ok what are the tests to check for keratoconus? I replied refraction with K values and corneal topography. Is the graft in left eye failed or is there a graft rejection? It was a tricky question. I said sir graft rejection is One of the reasons of graft failure but i would like to take the history n would like to know the time of surgery done to check for primary graft failure or late graft failure. I guess he understood i knew the concept. Ok last question, what would you do for corneal vascularisation? I said i can do cauterizatioan and sub-conj/intrastromal anti vegfs in addition to topical steroids. He smiled and replied im happy and patted on my back you can leave and then the bell rang.
**Case-3) Examiner said just give me the diagnosis:**

I told patient has endothelial keratoplasty and pseudophakic. He told me OK, what do you think is this graft clear? I said clear but he said Are you sure? Check again. I could not answer properly this question.

The clinical exam was over and i was still skeptical whether i would pass or not due to the neuro case till the result day… Finally on 23rd May result was published on my dashboard that dr dont worry you are now a fellow of RCPS glasgow. 😀 ALHAMDULILLAH!

sections.title: Dr. Ahsen's General Comments & Tips
content: 1. There is a grading system to evaluate candidate performance. You don’t need to answer every question to pass.

2. My single best advice is to keep calm during exam, it is a mind game as many past candidates said. One of my colleagues advised me to forget that you are in an exam and take it as a discussion with a senior colleague.
3. If you didn’t perform well in one station, keep fighting you still have the chance to pass if you perform well in other stations.
4. Practice clinical examination and master the techniques before the exam, just keep repeating again and again to master it.
5. Keep praying and prepare well and you will pass in sha Allah.
6. Definitely examiners are helpful, some examiners are not very helpful but I believe the examination system is fair and no one can fail you unless you perform poorly.

7. Do a lot of oral and clinical simulated exams, that’s the best way to be mentally and psychologically prepared. Sometimes you know a lot of information but you don’t know how to express it, simulated exams with study partners will help.
Feel Free to contact if I can help in anyway, All the best for all the candidates, definitely it is a tough journey but it is worth it.

sections.title: Dr. Amr Mohamed's FRCS Experience (April 2024)
sections.content: My Name Is Amr Mohamed, I am a pediatric ophthalmologist from Yemen. I passed the exam on the first attempt Alhamdulillah after a preparation of 2 months (3 weeks of vacation before the exam to fully concentrate on preparation).

sections.title: Study Sources - Dr. Mohamed
content: 1. Kanski 8th edition.
2. Practical Guide to VIVA and OSCE in Ophthalmology Examinations (Wong).
3. Internal medicine notes (Dr. Waleed Badr).
4. Previous Exam experiences (2015-2023) - the most valuable source (80% of exam from it), need to study and answer questions, find patterns and favorite questions, and stick to that.

5. Having A study partner, and 1 hour of daily practice, each participant prepares 3 questions (from past candidates’ experiences with answers) and asks each other. (Thanks to friends Dr. Mehmet from Turkey, Dr. Ahmed from Egypt, and other colleagues).
6. Clinical examination videos (Dr. Ayman Al Ghoneimy and Dr. Mohammed El Naggar) - check Dr. El Naggar’s Videos on YouTube (Arabic narration).
7. Dr. Ghada Zein El-Abedin's channel has a lot of valuable resources along with other exam experiences on YouTube.

sections.title: Viva Examination (23/4/2024) - Dr. Mohamed
sections.content: This section covers the viva examination for Dr. Mohamed.

sections.title: First Station: General Medicine & Neurology - Viva
content: **1. (written scenario) History of a patient undergoing cataract surgery who was found to have atrial fibrillation. What will you do?**

I told him that I needed to know whether it was acute atrial fibrillation or chronic and the patient would need beta blockers like Esmolol, in addition to Digoxin, and if no improvement the patient would need cardioversion whether electric cardioversion or drug cardioversion with amiodarone and also patient need anticoagulant like warfarin. The examiner asked me what other drugs were for anticoagulation. He asked me about the causes of atrial fibrillation.
**2. (written scenario) You Have a patient who has a cataract and plans to do cataract surgery and he is on warfarin. What will you do?**

I told him that we can plan the surgery under topical anesthesia or subtenon anesthesia to avoid risk of retrobulbar hemorrhages and we can do clear corneal incision. I don't know if he wants something else, but he did not comment at all. I would coordinate with the physician whether we can stop warfarin or give another anticoagulant.
**3. (written scenario) Female with Galactorrhea and Amenorrhea, what is the diagnosis?**

I told him that the patient is having chiasmatic lesion mostly pituitary adenoma. Then he said what are you going to do (examination and investigations)? I told him anterior segment, posterior segment, check the optic disc, check the pupillary reaction and check the confrontation visual field and visual field test (automated perimetry). We need to do a neuroimaging, brain MRI and hormonal essay for the prolactin and other pituitary hormones. Then, I asked about expected visual field defect? I told him that Bitemporal hemianopia usually starting with the superior field. Then he asked me what drugs can you give for this patient? I told him bromocriptine or cabergoline. Then he said other options? I told if the patient is still having complaints or there is progressive visual field loss, then we can proceed for surgery. Then he said what is the surgery? I told transsphenoidal hypophysectomy, he said Any other options? I stereotactic radiotherapy. I think he wanted something else, but I didn't know. Then he said post-surgery the patient developed polyuria. What is the problem? I couldn’t answer properly.

**4. A case scenario of a patient with diplopia and ptosis (I forgot the main scenario) but the questions were about myasthenia gravis, the clinical tests and the pharmacological tests, tensilon test specifically in details.**
**5. (written scenario) A case of five-year-old patient child with vision 6/6 and 6/18. What are you going to do?**

I told him. Anterior segment, posterior segment, cover tests, extraocular motility, cycloplegic refraction, The Examiner said everything is normal. Then I told him it could be amblyopia, then examiner asked what is amblyopia and what are the types of amblyopia and what are you going to do? I told him I will give glasses if any significant refractive error or anisometropia, and amblyopia therapy, he asked would you do amblyopia therapy immediately? Then asked about Amblyopia therapy modalities? I told him patching of the good eye, four to five hours. He said that the patient's five-year-old would you start the patching directly, I said yes immediately. he said OK, what are the other options? I told him atropine drops. what is that called? I said penalization.
**6. (written scenario) Patient three-year old with acute onset of convergent strabismus for one month, he told me what are the differential diagnoses?**

I told him acute esotropia and accommodative esotropia. What else? 6th cranial nerve palsy. what are you going to do? I mentioned full examination including cover tests, extraocular motility to differentiate whether it is comitant or incomitant, pupillary reflexes, anterior segment and posterior segment, cycloplegic refraction, he said. What is the most common cause in this age group? I told accommodative ET, what are you going to do for this? I told him full cycloplegic hypermetropic refraction glasses and treat amblyopia If there is any fixation preference.
**7. (written scenario) It was elderly patient with lateral rectus paralysis, what are you going to do?**

I said I will ask history about any systemic diseases and history of the onset, progression and the duration, measuring the angle and checking the other cranial nerve, anterior & posterior segment examinations, pupillary examination. Then he said what are the investigations would you do? I told him about investigations such as blood sugar and lipid profile, neuroimaging also, how would you manage? I told we can do patching of one of the eyes or prism glasses, He said OK The patient came after six months with the same deviation. I told him if deviation is stable, we can proceed with strabismus surgery, he said. What else? I told him botulinum toxin but usually after six months, it is not effective because of medial rectus restriction. And he said what else? I told Fresnel prisms.

sections.title: DDx: Acute Convergent Strabismus in a Child

branches: Sixth Cranial Nerve Palsy (Abduction deficit, incomitant)
Ophthalmo Pearl: A thorough cycloplegic refraction is crucial for diagnosis and management of accommodative esotropia.

sections.title: 2nd Station: Anterior Segment & Oculoplasty - Viva
content: **1. (written scenario) Patient who will do a cataract surgery under local anesthesia. What are the historical points that is important?**

I told some of them like systemic diseases. Then I asked about the onset, progression, duration of the cataract. Any pain? Any other complaints? Anterior segment, Posterior segment? Intraocular pressure, Check the other eye, ask about history of trauma, check the pupils, check the extraocular motility. He kept saying what else, what else? I think there is one table in Kansky (lens chapter) that have a lot of things regarding preoperative assessment (respiratory disease, rheumatoid arthritis, etc. Then he asked about the examination. I told him also that during the evaluation I want to evaluate whether the patients fit for local anesthesia or not. because in some cases like patients with parkinsonism or seizures it is not possible.
**2. A photograph of a child with left leukocoria. He said, what is this?**

I told him left leukocoria and told him the differential diagnosis. Then he said, OK, if this is PHPV, what are you going to do? I said it depends whether it is anterior PHPV or posterior PHPV. If Anterior PHPV we can do cataract surgery with a guarded visual prognosis said, what are you going to counsel the patient’s family about? I told him about visual prognosis and need of amblyopia therapy post operatively and risk of glaucoma, retinal detachment. I mentioned also approach to a case of leukocoria regarding EUA and B scan ultrasonography.
**3. How would you counsel a patient for cataract surgery?**

I will tell the patient there is a risk of PCR, not putting IOL, Risk of endophthalmitis, bullous keratopathy, glaucoma, and persistent uveitis. Risk of rupture group or retrobulbar hemorrhage from anesthesia.

**4. The examiner handed me a photo of lower lid basal cell carcinoma. It was rodent ulcer So asking me to describe? what is the most probable diagnosis, how would you treat and details about the reconstruction?**
**5. A question about dry eye disease. Slit lamp photo of a patient with rose Bengal stain, asked describe and what other stains that can be used? And what is another test of dry eye?**

I mentioned tear break up time. Schirmer test 1 & 2. tear meniscus height. Then asked how would you treat this patient? I told if there is any systemic disease we need to treat the underlying cause. Then we can start with environmental changes with lid hygiene, frequent blinking, and goggles. Then I talked about artificial tears. If no improvement, we can shift to preservative-free artificial tears with topical steroid and cyclosporin. I told him also about punctual plugs, he said, what is the systemic treatment that can be given. I told him doxycycline for meibomian gland dysfunction but I think he wanted also other things. Then I said we can do surgeries if the patient is having any disease like entropion or trichiasis or ectropion.
**6. Then he gave a photo of an elderly female closing her eyes forcefully and there was left lagophthalmos, he asked what it is and what is the most probable diagnosis.**

Told there is lagophthalmos and most probably there is facial nerve palsy because there was also mouth deviation. And then he said, OK, what are you going to do? I said refer to neurologist Then for the eye temporary measures we can give lubricant eyedrops, lubricant ointments, eyelid tapping. Then if it is permanent facial nerve palsy like compressing lesion or permanent damage of the nerve then we can do permanent measures, He said What are those measures? I told medial canthoplasty, lateral tarsorrhaphy, gold weight implant. Then he said do you do those procedures by yourself? I said no, and he also told me what about botulinum toxin? I said yes, we can give botulinum toxin and he said in those patients usually what they have tearing or dryness, I said tearing. He said why? I said because of punctal eversion and reflex tearing. He then said if you are not doing those surgeries by yourself, what are you going to do? I said I would refer patient to oculoplastic surgeon? He said OK.
**7. (case scenario) A case of a child with lid swelling and redness for two days.**

I answered it might be preseptal cellulitis, orbital cellulitis or conjunctivitis. Then asked how to differentiate orbital from preseptal cellulitis? then next question was if it is a case of orbital cellulitis what are you going to do? I told him admission, CBC to check WBC's temperature, ENT consultation, CT orbit & sinuses to check if there is a subperiosteal Abscess and to differentiate whether it's preseptal or orbital. Also, clinical signs of orbital cellulitis like proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, optic nerve affection, and pupils.

sections.title: DDx: Child with Lid Swelling and Redness

rows: Swelling/redness anterior to orbital septum, no proptosis, no ophthalmoplegia, normal vision, normal pupils.
Proptosis, pain with eye movements, ophthalmoplegia, reduced vision, RAPD, fever, malaise, often associated with sinusitis.
Conjunctival hyperemia, discharge, usually bilateral, no lid swelling/redness beyond conjunctiva, no proptosis.

sections.title: Third Station: Posterior Segment & Glaucoma - Viva
content: **1. He asked are you doing trabeculectomy? I said no, but I observed a trab before. He said OK if you did trab and post op day One, patient has AC shallow and IOP 3 mm Hg. What are you going to do?**

I said I need to assess first the degree of AC shallowness whether it is grade 1,2,3 whether it is iridocorneal or pupillo-corneal or lenticulo-corneal. Then I need to check seidel test whether positive or negative, assess bleb height, Differential it might be over filtration or bleb leak or ciliary shutdown. Then I said also I need to check the fundus. Then he said could it be a choroidal detachment? I said yes, it could be choroidal detachment. Then asked what are you going to do? I said that we can give bandage contact lens but he said bandage contact lens will not be enough and it will not sit properly. I said, OK, we can do patching he said. What else? I said we can decrease the steroid, increase the antibiotic eye drops, Said OK, what else? Then I did a mistake. I said we can do drainage for the choroidal detachment; he was not happy with that.

**2. Then he asked me another scenario, if the patient also with trabeculectomy and post operatively, he has a pressure 70 mm Hg. I said, OK, we have 3 possibilities whether 1. pupillary block and it can be checked with transillumination, 2. suprachoroidal hemorrhage and it can be checked with B scan or from examination. And the third possibility is malignant glaucoma or aqueous misdirection said, OK, it’s is malignant glaucoma. What are you going to do?**

I said cycloplegic eye drops, he said Did you see malignant glaucoma this before? I said yes, he said. Do they benefit from cycloplegic eyedrops? I said mostly no, but it can help some of the patients. I forgot actually to mention antiglaucoma groups. Then he said, what else? I said if the patient is pseudophakic, yag laser posterior capsulotomy and hyaloidotomy can be done. And if the patient is phakic, we can also do YAG laser through PI. Otherwise, I would refer the patient to VR surgeon, to do vitrectomy.
**3. A patient with primary open angle glaucoma. For example, patient is having IOP 30 mm Hg. What are you going to give him?**

I told him we can start him with the one antiglaucoma eye drops Whether beta blocker if There are no contraindications like Timolol 0.5% twice daily or we can give prostaglandin analogues Latanoprost, Travoprost or Bimatoprost once daily at bed time. He said OKAY after giving your patient prostaglandin analogues and What are you going to tell him? I said about the complications. Like red eye, trichomegaly, Iris hyperpigmentation and I told him about counselling the patient that he needed to know that he needed to comply to this eye drops for the rest of the life because it is a progressive and chronic disease. He said OK patient was not comfortable. Then I said I can shift to another antiglaucoma. He said OK patient is not tolerant to any anti glaucoma eye drops. I said we can do laser trabeculoplasty said he don't want laser. Then I said preservative free anti glaucoma and that was the answer he was looking for.
**4. Fourth question: A photo of a patient with the central retinal artery occlusion with cilioretinal artery sparing, he said What are you going to do?**

I said about the emergency treatment, breathing in a paper bag, carbogen, antiglaucoma, ocular massage, paracentesis, also checking the other eye and referring the patient urgently to internist to do investigations like Carotid Doppler ultrasound and echocardiogram.
**5. The examiner asked about VMT case (OCT Macula picture) what is the treatment?**

I said it depends on the vision and the visual symptoms. If the patient has good vision and no metamorphopsia then we can observe the patient because some of the cases will improve spontaneously. If the vision is worsening or there is a severe metamorphosis, then we can do pars plana vitrectomy with membrane removal and sometimes with ILM peeling. The examiner stopped here.
**6. A patient having rheumatoid arthritis and he's taking systemic medications. What are the drugs that can affect the eye?**

I said about the steroids causing posterior subcapsular cataract and glaucoma and increase the risk of infections. Then I talked about hydroxychloroquine and she asked about Bull’s eye maculopathy and how to diagnose? how to screen the patient? Patient evaluation? what is the toxic dose and what are the condition that if the patient is having risk of drug toxicity will increase. It was renal disease, but I couldn't answer that.

**7. A photo of glaucomatous optic disk. It was a large disk with large vertical cupping with peripapillary atrophy, nasalization of the optic disc and bayonetting. Then examiner said what are you going to do for this patient?**

I said full evaluation of the glaucoma. She stressed on the role of the central corneal thickness and the importance. I talked about underestimation and what is the normal corneal thickness, investigations like visual field, OCT nerve fiber layer.

sections.title: Clinical Examination (25/4/2024) - Dr. Mohamed
sections.content: This section details the clinical examination stations on the second day of Dr. Mohamed's exam.

sections.title: First Station (Oculoplasty) - Clinicals
content: **1. A 45-year-old Female with bilateral dermatochalasis and ptosis. Examiner Just said EXAMINE, I started by observation I can see bilateral ptosis and dermatochalasis. He said OK. I said I want to examine ptosis. He said proceed. So, I did the MRD1 It was -1 in right eye and 2mm in the left eye. Then Palpebral fissure height height, then Levator function and Lid crease. Then I told him I want to check lagophthalmos. I did it. Then Bell's phenomena. Then I told him corneal sensation. Then I told him I want to check for the cause. I told him I want to do fatigability test. He said how? I said I will let the patient to look up for 30 seconds then I will repeat the measurements of ptosis. Also, I can do ice test or sleep test. He said what are investigations that can be done? I said acetylcholine receptor antibodies and EMG single fiber and edrophonium test or neostigmine test. what is the result in single fiber EMG? I could not answer. Then asked how will you treat myasthenia gravis? I told him patient will need pyridostigmine and oral steroids in some cases and I would refer the patient to a neurologist for further evaluation and management.**

**2. Examiner asked me to examine patient’s right eye using slit lamp. I checked the eye there was an ACIOL with deep AC, clear cornea. I told the findings. Then I stopped examination. Then he told me this is oculoplastic session, please look again at the eye. When I looked again, I looked at the lids and I found I found DCR tube. Asked what are the indications for DCR and what are the complications of DCR.**

**3. Third case was a young male patient with right eye Phthisis Bulbi. He told me examine with the torch and he told me what is this? I told Phthisis Bulbi. He said why that can happen. I told the chronic endophthalmitis post intraocular surgery or severe trauma. He said OK look again and check what is the cause. I checked again I could not answer what is the specific cause for the case. Then he told me OK what are you going to do for him? I told him for Cosmesis we can give colored contact lenses or prosthetic shell or because of the loss of orbital volume, we can go for evisceration with orbital implant and prosthetic shell. Time UP.**

sections.title: The Second Station (Anterior Segment) - Clinicals
content: **1. Examine Left eye. clear cornea and two sutures and irregular pupil with a slightly inferiorly subluxated scleral fixation IOL. AC reaction +1.**

The examiner asked what could happen to the patient? I told maybe a traumatic cataract and there was no capsular support or maybe the patient was pseudophakic and IOL dislocated, then second surgery done or third scenario that it might be a primary aphakia and secondary scleral fixation IOL because there is no support. He said, OK, what are the things that you want to examine? I said intraocular pressure and fundus. He said why intraocular pressure? I said that the patient might have a glaucoma from the main cause of the trauma. If it is a traumatic case maybe like cyclodialysis or angle recession He said what else I couldn't answer. He said you mentioned there is AC reaction. I answered it might be uveitic glaucoma. Then asked for IOL subluxation what are you going to do? I said I will check the vision. If vision is good then only conservatively managed with glasses. If vision is bad then patient might need contact lenses or refractive surgery.

**2. An elderly patient with pseudophakic bullous keratopathy. He had a large superior corneal wound. Maybe intra capsular or extra capsular cataract extraction. There was a large part of iris loss superiorly from 8:00 to 2:00 and patient had pseudophakic bullous keratopathy with a central epithelial defect. I mentioned the findings. He said what could happen to the patient. I said maybe intra capsular cataract extraction complicated or extra capsular cataract extraction complicated without IOL.**

Then Asked what are you going to do for the patient? I said if IOP and B scan is normal then we can proceed for graft. He said what type of graft? I said whether penetrating keratoplasty or endothelial keratoplasty, depending on the level of stromal scarring, if it is full thickness then we will need penetrating keratoplasty. Then he said, OK, what else? I said also IOL implantation. I told him whether we do staged procedure, graft first, then IOL or a Combined procedure. he asked me about the advantages of each procedure. I told him then he said OK if you did not put IOL only graft what can be done? I couldn’t answer. he said OK you can use contact lens for correction rather than doing second surgery.

**3. Examiner said just give me the diagnosis. I told patient has endothelial keratoplasty and pseudophakic. He told me OK, what do you think is this graft clear? I said clear but he said Are you sure? Check again. I could not answer properly this question.**

sections.title: Third Station (Posterior Segment) - Clinicals
content: **1. Examine with 90 D lens. Patient had a full thickness macular hole and all the area surrounding the hole it was pigmented so it was not a clear hole.**

I told him it is full thickness macular hole. He said what is the grading of the macular hole and what are the causes of macular hole and what is the surgery for macular hole and what are the complications of gas injection and what are the precautions that you will give to the patient post gas injection? I said face down and no air travel.

**2. Examine with indirect Ophthalmoscope. patient had the pale optic disc with regressed fibrovascular membrane in front of the disc and 360 laser marks. So I told the findings. He said what could be the cause I told I want to check the other eye. He said that it has the same findings. Then I said it might be a case of stable proliferative diabetic retinopathy.**

He said OK, I mentioned also that the patient is pseudophakic. Examiner asked what are the indications for vitrectomy in diabetes? I told persistent vitreous hemorrhage or tractional detachment threatening the macula or combined retinal tractional detachment with rhegmatogenous detachment. He said, OK, this patient is vitrectomized. Did you see silicone? I said no, I could not see silicone. He said OK, what are the complications of silicon oil in vitrectomy? Then I said glaucoma, band keratopathy. Then asked about for how long you should keep the silicone? I said ideally between three and six months but sometimes we need longer tamponade in some cases. Then the other examiner asked me about PRP laser, how to do PRP laser. Then I told him the settings and how many spots. Then asked about macular edema. If the patient is having macular edema, I told I need to give intravitreal injection. He said what are the types of intravitreal injection? I told Bevacizumab, Ranibizumab and Aflibercept. Then the other examiner told me if the patient is having macular edema and vitreomacular traction, what can you do? I said the intravitreal injections is contraindicated. laser might increase traction as well, then we can do vitrectomy to remove the membrane and to improve the macular edema.
**3. Examine with 90D this child (8 OR 9 year-old- boy). He told me spot diagnosis?**
The disc was really very strange. I didn't reach the diagnosis. I told maybe it is a congenital optic disc anomaly might be morning glory or optic disc coloboma or glaucomatous optic disc. Time UP.

sections.title: Fourth Station (Neurology & Ocular Motility) - Clinicals
content: **1. 15-year-old Male with Exotropia. He told me to examine extraocular motility. I told him I want to do cover /uncover Test first. He said OK so I did the cover tests at near and at distance patient has alternating exotropia. Then I said I want to measure the deviation. He said OK go ahead. He gave me prism bar and I did measurement for the deviation. It was 35 prism diopter exotropia. Then he asked me do you want to measure deviation without glasses. I told him OK. Then I asked the patient can you see without glasses. He said I cannot see. Then I just did Hirschberg and I told him almost the same angle. Then I checked the motility. Patient had inferior oblique overaction in both eyes. Then he told me what are you going to do? I said I will do full examination including anterior & posterior segment, give glasses and treat amblyopia if present then check then I will do surgery.**

**2. Middle Aged woman, examine pupils I checked for heterochromia and anisocoria in light, then asked to switch off the light and checked anisocoria in dark. Then I checked direct and consensual light reflex and swinging flashlight test. I noticed Grade 1 RAPD in the left eye from the second attempt. Then examiner asked what you want to do? I told I want to check the fundus. He said OK check it. I checked patient had the cupped disc and disc and pallor. I told him it might be glaucomatous optic neuropathy. He said check the other eye. other eye disc was normal. Then he told me what it could be. I could not answer properly. He asked me what are the types of optic atrophy. I told him primary, secondary and consecutive optic atrophy. Then he told me this is which one. I could not answer properly his questions.**

**3. Then Examiner asked me to perform confrontation visual field test for a third patient. I just started with the beginning of the visual field. Then the bell rang and I could not complete the case.**

content: 1. There is a grading system to evaluate candidate performance. You don’t need to answer every question to pass.

2. My single best advice is to keep calm during exam, it is a mind game as many past candidates said. One of my colleagues advised me to forget that you are in an exam and take it as a discussion with a senior colleague.
3. If you didn’t perform well in one station, keep fighting you still have the chance to pass if you perform well in other stations.
4. Practice clinical examination and master the techniques before the exam, just keep repeating again and again to master it.
5. Keep praying and prepare well and you will pass in sha Allah.
6. Definitely examiners are helpful, some examiners are not very helpful but I believe the examination system is fair and no one can fail you unless you perform poorly.

7. Do a lot of oral and clinical simulated exams, that’s the best way to be mentally and psychologically prepared. Sometimes you know a lot of information but you don’t know how to express it, simulated exams with study partners will help.
Feel Free to contact if I can help in anyway, All the best for all the candidates, definitely it is a tough journey but it is worth it.

sections.title: Dr. Sumeet Lahane's FRCS Experience (Nov 2024)
sections.content: Dr. Sumeet Lahane shares his FRCS 3 Glasgow experience at Aditya Jyoti Eye Hospital, Mumbai, on 12-14 November 2024.

sections.title: Preparation & Suggestions - Dr. Lahane
content: **Preparation:**
- Wong
- FRCS cakewalk
- FAQ DNB
- I courses series
**Suggestions:**

- Please do see I courses examination techniques and practise them in your daily clinic (There are also techniques available on Chuas website and various you tube portals but in I courses they are very well compiled at one place).
- From all lectures of I courses of clinical cases do take out extensive and important notes which will help you to revise.
- This is specially very useful if you are in time crunch or unable to cope up with extensive reading schedule with your daily work.
- Please do have a study partner/partners with whom you can discuss regularly.
- Please do talk to your friends, colleagues who have cleared exam so they can guide you positively.

sections.title: 12 November - Table Vivas - Dr. Lahane
sections.content: 3 stations - Each station 2 examiners. 20 minutes on one table, 60 mins total. Each examiner discusses 3-4 case scenarios (written on cardboard handed over to candidate) in 10 mins. After 10 mins bell second examiner takes over.

sections.title: Station One: Neurophthal, Motility and Medicine - Viva
content: 1. Patient sitting and waiting for cataract got Seizures - Types, Etiology, Management.
2. Optic neuritis in 30 year old male - Causes other than demyelination, And risk of recurrence.
3. Esotropia in six month old child - Management.
4. Sixth nerve palsy causes - Importance of age in same.
5. Old age patient with sudden Ptosis unilateral which is worse during day and intermittent diplopia - differential of Ptosis and myasthenia diagnosis.

sections.title: Station Two: Anterior Segment and Eyelids - Viva
content: 1. Uveitis cataract - what precautions to be taken pre, intra and - they wanted to know about CME.
2. Management of small pupil during cataract surgery.
3. Shallow AC during cataract surgery - DDs and management.
4. Wanted to know about expulsive choroidal hemorrhage.
5. Caustic soda injury - wanted to know about depth of injury, PH, sequelae - Symblepharon (kept asking how much TIME you will wash even after telling litmus test).
6. Eyelid mass - Keratocanthoma - but give all DD.
7. Conjunctival Nevus.

sections.title: Station Three: Posterior Segment and Glaucoma - Viva
content: 1. Shallow AC post Trab.
2. Glaucoma disc picture - wanted all the details about alpha and beta zone.
3. 88 year old patient one eyed - unable to tolerate glaucoma medications - Rx options - surgery, laser - went in detail about SLT and advantages and disadvantages.
4. CHRPE - types, Till when you will follow up.
5. RP with ? CNVM ? - Went to findings on ERG, Other than ERG what investigations You can do to early detect RP.

sections.title: 14 November - Clinical Examination - Dr. Lahane
sections.content: This section details the clinical examination stations for Dr. Lahane.

sections.title: Station One: Neuro Ophthal Station - Clinicals
content: 1. Child with RE eso - Asked to check motility. First check vision and do motility - bilateral restriction of lateral gaze with change in palpebral fissure - Bilateral Duans with ESO. Do say that would like to do cover uncover prior to motility - they may say no and do directly motility. Asked management, amblyopia and differential diagnosis.

2. Young patient - check pupil. RE RAPD with irregular pupil. Asked to check fields. Only on RE checking got to know restricted fields - tunnel vision. Causes asked for irregular pupil with RAPD - a case of RE traumatic glaucoma with sphincter tear and ? Angle recession.

sections.title: Station Two: Oculoplasty and Lid - Clinicals
content: 1. Bilateral proptosis - asked to examine. Discussion on hertel. Pt also had exotropia. So while doing hertel of RE to close LE so RE takes fixation otherwise can not measure in such cases (patient was also aware as when I tried closing her other eye she herself did it). Do comment on hertel base.
2. Bilateral Ptosis - mostly aponeurotic - do talk about myasthenia also. Management, Complications.
3. Facial palsy right side - tell only observation findings. What’s the management of acute - bell rang.

sections.title: Station Three: Anterior Segment - Clinicals
content: 1. Lady with LE PCIOL, PI marks, large PI and failed bleb and RE also PI with shallow anterior chamber. What will you do for her. Spoke about surgeries and laser but they wanted something which is more of office based? They expected needling. There was no suture on bleb and apparently old failed bleb.
2. Young male with full thickness graft with SFIOL - why was graft done and findings.
3. Young female with ectasia both eye and scar. Management of both eyes for vision. Discussion on scleral lenses and DALK.

sections.title: Station Four: Posterior Segment - Clinicals
content: 1. Diabetic retinopathy - PRP marks and haemorrhages - laser stable PDR with macular edema - management of central involving and non involving macular edema. Long term prognosis - counselling and physician reference.
2. Macular hole - bad prognosis indicators on clinical examination. Full thickness or partial thickness differences.
3. Retinitis pigmentosa - long term prognosis, family genetics. Treatment of macular edema.

sections.title: OSCE Exam-2024 (Unnamed Candidate)
sections.content: This section outlines the OSCE experience of an unnamed candidate from 2024.

sections.title: Anterior Segment - OSCE
content: **Case 1:** Subconj silicon, aphakic, with peaked distorted pupil, loose corneal suture, AC cells, what do you want to do for this pt?
**Case 2:** Dislocated IOL with optic in the AC and pupillary block and iris bombe and PAS, pigments on the IOL, what are the effects of this condition? What do you want to do?

**Case 3:** Trichiasis, PKP in a pseudophakic eye, what do you think happened? I said corneal decompensation after cataract surgery or planned triple procedure then I asked to examine the other eye, I couldn’t see anything (other candidates say she had guttata).

sections.title: Posterior Segment - OSCE
content: **Case 1:** TRD in one eye, with PRP marks and hard exudates in the macula? What investigations do u want to do to check if it’s clinically significant? examine the other eye I saw NVD.
**Case 2:** ERM.
**Case 3:** A very vague case huge whitish lesion inferiorly with PRP marks also, centrally retina was elevated & examiner wanted me to say hole (I think) but I couldn’t see any holes.

sections.title: Neuro - OSCE
content: **Case 1:** Examine the pupil, it showed right RAPD, then he told me do confrontation to the other eye, it showed constricted field with only central vision preserved, what do u think of the case? He wanted Advanced glaucoma.
**Case 2:** A girl with alternating XT cover tests & motility.

sections.title: Oculoplasty - OSCE
content: **Case 1:** Involutional Ptosis in one eye more than the other, how to examine (all the ptosis sheet) what procedure you want to do?
**Case 2:** Measure the proptosis in left eye (it was pseudo) right eye had enophthalmos and PESS and discussion about how to evaluate the ocular prosthesis.
**Case 3:** Very narrow palpebral fissure with a bony lesion superotemporal, UL madarosis, distortion, ulceration at the lid margin (it was a weird case).
